chapter: Kansas City, Basie, Prez and Booker Pittman
title: Booker Pittman's lost six years in South America
summary: Booker tells Budd he lost six years cutting cane in South America in a daze before recovering and becoming a star bandleader.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Yes. Of course this was many years

later. I hadn't seen Booker in a long time. In fact, when I had joined Earl HInes later -- I'll get back to my story, but I have to say this in order to clarify some points that Mr. (Hinton) has asked me.

I was in Tuskegee, and of course his mother had then, after she had lost her husband, and that (inaudible) and she had gone back to Tuskegee where -- which her father founded, and she was teaching music there, and I happened to be there with Earl Fatha Hines, and I think this was around 1937, and she had told me that she don't hear from her son very much, and she heard he was very ill, and whatnot, and of course I was concerned, because Booker and I were raised together.

So later on, very late, very, very, very later, Booker came back to the United States, and he brought his wife and daughter with him, and his daughter's a very, very, very great, great, great singer, and artist, and in Rio de Janeiro, and when I was down there I saw her, but anyway, they came in and I signed the papers. (He) had been on the Jack Paar show, and then Booker, of course, got in touch with me, and I signed for her to stay in this country where I would be responsible for her while she was here.

So in themeantime I had them out to the house, and Booker told me of his disappearance. He told me that he finally came to his senses one day, and learned that he had been working in a cane patch, cutting cane in South America,

for six years, and he don't remember anything in between. He was like a Zombie. He had gotten high off something that they give him down there, and his mind was completely gone. And that he finally came to one day, and that's how he met his step-daughter's mother. She had been married to a diplomat of South America, and he finally got away from this plantation that they had him on, and he remembered that he was a musician.

So he got hold of a clarinet some kind of a way, and he started to play, and everybody really dug him. Before this, mind you, he had been a big band leader all over South America, with a big band. He had made success, and all of a sudden he tripped up some kind of way and six years out of his life was gone. Now he's like coming through out of a coma, out of a sleep, and he told me, and he said that he began to put the pieces back together, and started to play.

Then he met this woman, and then she saw the great talent that he had, and then she kind of put him back on his feet. And then him and his daughter -- he started pushing her, and whatnot, and then she became a big star. They worked together. He was singing like Pops, and he did the thing, he came to New York. We made a recording together with Frank Driggs, up to Columbia, and we recorded 13th and Lydia, the place that I was talking about in the interview with Milt.
